events.title: Trump Signs Space Policy Directive 1
events.detail: President Trump signed SPD-1, "Reinvigorating America's Human Space Exploration Program," officially redirecting NASA back to the Moon. It amended the 2010 National Space Policy, tasking NASA to lead a program to return humans to the Moon and eventually reach Mars. This act marked the official genesis of what would become the Artemis program.

events.title: NASA Announces 'Moon to Mars' Campaign and Deep Space Gateway
events.detail: NASA formally branded its exploration strategy as 'Moon to Mars' and announced the Deep Space Gateway — a proposed small station in lunar orbit. In the FY2019 budget request, the name shifted to Lunar Orbital Platform-Gateway (LOP-G), signaling a structured international partnership model. International partners ESA, JAXA, and CSA expressed interest in contributing hardware.

sources.name: Planetary Society Moon to Mars Overview

events.title: VP Pence Issues 2024 Moon Landing Mandate
events.detail: Vice President Mike Pence, speaking at the fifth National Space Council meeting, directed NASA to land American astronauts on the Moon within five years — by 2024 — four years ahead of schedule. He declared NASA would use 'any means necessary,' including commercial rockets, and warned that contractors unable to meet the goal would be replaced. This political mandate became the forcing function for the entire accelerated Artemis program.

events.title: NASA Names Lunar Return Program 'Artemis'
events.detail: NASA Administrator Jim Bridenstine officially named the lunar return program 'Artemis,' after the Greek goddess twin sister of Apollo and goddess of the Moon. The name carried a deliberate commitment to land the first woman on the Moon. Bridenstine set 2024 as the target for the crewed lunar landing, with commercial and international partners as core elements of the architecture.

events.title: NASA Awards 11 HLS Study Contracts Under NextSTEP
events.detail: NASA awarded 11 study contracts under the Next Space Technologies for Exploration Partnerships (NextSTEP) program for the Human Landing System. These initial studies began the formal commercial lunar lander competition that would eventually lead to the SpaceX and Blue Origin contracts. Industry teams explored crewed lunar descent and ascent vehicles capable of landing near the south pole.

events.title: NASA Awards HLS Phase 1 Contracts ($967M Total)
events.detail: NASA selected three industry teams for 10-month HLS design contracts totaling ~$967 million: Blue Origin's National Team (with Lockheed Martin, Northrop Grumman, Draper, and L3Harris), Dynetics (with Sierra Nevada), and SpaceX's Starship variant. Each team would develop full-scale lander concepts before a final down-select to an operational contract.

events.title: Northrop Grumman Wins Gateway HALO Design Contract ($187M)
events.detail: NASA signed a $187 million contract with Northrop Grumman to complete the preliminary design of HALO (Habitation and Logistics Outpost), Gateway's pressurized crew habitat. NASA also announced that HALO would be co-manifested with Maxar's Power and Propulsion Element (PPE) on a single Falcon Heavy, saving the cost of a separate rocket. This established the combined PPE+HALO as Gateway's first element.

events.title: Artemis Accords Signed by 8 Founding Nations
events.detail: NASA and the U.S. State Department launched the Artemis Accords with 8 founding nations: Australia, Canada, Italy, Japan, Luxembourg, UAE, UK, and the United States. The non-binding accords established principles for peaceful, transparent, and sustainable space exploration including interoperability, deconfliction of activities, and information sharing. China and Russia notably declined to sign, framing their own lunar programs outside the U.S.-led framework.

events.title: Trump Signs SPD-6: Space Nuclear Power & Propulsion Strategy
events.detail: President Trump signed Space Policy Directive 6, directing NASA and the Department of Energy to develop a fission surface power system demonstrable on the Moon by 2027 and scalable for Mars. SPD-6 also covered nuclear thermal propulsion for future deep-space missions. NASA Administrator Bridenstine called nuclear power 'fundamentally enabling' for sustained lunar presence and eventual Mars missions.

events.title: SLS Green Run Hot Fire Test 1 — Partial (67 Seconds)
events.detail: At Stennis Space Center, engineers ignited all four SLS RS-25 engines simultaneously for the first time, but the test was aborted at 67.7 seconds (target: ~500 seconds) when Engine #4 triggered a Major Component Failure indication. Investigation traced the abort to a conservatively set hydraulic parameter in the test stand, not an actual engine defect. A second full-duration test was immediately planned.

sources.name: American Astronautical Society Green Run Report

events.title: SLS Green Run Hot Fire Test 2 — Full Success (499 Seconds)
events.detail: The second Green Run static fire at Stennis Space Center B-2 test stand ran the full 8 minutes 19 seconds (499 seconds), firing all four RS-25 engines and generating 1.6 million pounds of thrust. All secondary objectives — engine gimballing, throttle profiles — were met. SLS Program Manager John Honeycutt declared the core stage earned 'an A-plus.' The test cleared SLS to ship to Kennedy Space Center for flight processing.

events.title: SpaceX Wins Sole HLS Contract — $2.89 Billion
events.detail: NASA selected only SpaceX's Starship HLS for the full Human Landing System development contract, valued at $2.89 billion. NASA stated it preferred two contractors but Congress had not appropriated sufficient funds. The contract covered one uncrewed lunar landing demonstration and one crewed Artemis III landing. Blue Origin and Dynetics were not selected, triggering immediate protest actions by both firms.

events.title: Blue Origin Files GAO Protest and Federal Lawsuit Over HLS
events.detail: Blue Origin and Dynetics protested the sole-source HLS award to the GAO on April 26. After GAO denied both protests in July 2021, Blue Origin sued NASA in the U.S. Court of Federal Claims in August. NASA paused SpaceX HLS work while litigation proceeded. Jeff Bezos personally offered over $3 billion to NASA to secure a second lander contract. A federal judge dismissed Blue Origin's suit on November 4, and SpaceX work resumed.

events.title: SLS Core Stage Arrives at Kennedy Space Center
events.detail: After shipping from Stennis Space Center, the SLS core stage arrived at KSC for vehicle integration in the Vehicle Assembly Building. By June 12, NASA announced the fully stacked Artemis I SLS/Orion vehicle assembly was complete, with the 322-foot rocket ready for further pre-launch processing. This was the first fully assembled Moon rocket at KSC since Apollo 17 in 1972.

events.title: SLS Exploration Upper Stage Passes Critical Design Review
events.detail: The Critical Design Review for the Exploration Upper Stage (EUS) was completed, clearing SLS Block 1B development to proceed to hardware fabrication. The EUS, powered by four RL10C-3 engines, would increase SLS payload capacity from 27 to 38 metric tons to trans-lunar injection — enabling Orion to carry co-manifested Gateway payloads. The EUS cost, originally $962M in 2017, would later balloon to nearly $2.8 billion before cancellation in 2026.

events.title: Artemis I Rolls Out to Launch Pad 39B for First Time
events.detail: The fully stacked Artemis I SLS/Orion vehicle — 322 feet tall, 5.75 million pounds — rolled out of the VAB to Launch Pad 39B over approximately 11 hours on the crawler-transporter. This was the first Moon rocket rollout since Apollo 17 in December 1972. The milestone began the Artemis I launch campaign and opened the wet dress rehearsal phase.

events.title: Three Wet Dress Rehearsal Attempts Face Propellant Leak Issues
events.detail: NASA attempted three wet dress rehearsals between April and May 2022, each encountering problems: a liquid hydrogen leak on April 1 cut short the first attempt; propellant loading cutoff on April 14 ended the second; an unresolved hydrogen leak ended the third. The rocket was rolled back to the VAB for repairs, delaying launch from spring to late summer/fall 2022. A successful full WDR was finally completed on June 20, 2022.

events.title: Artemis I Launch Scrub #1 — Faulty Engine Temperature Sensor
events.detail: The first Artemis I launch attempt was scrubbed at T-40 minutes due to a faulty temperature sensor on RS-25 Engine #3, which appeared not to have reached its required pre-chill temperature. Engineers determined the sensor itself was faulty, not the engine, but could not safely proceed. A second launch attempt was scheduled for September 3.

events.title: Artemis I Launch Scrub #2 — Liquid Hydrogen Leak
events.detail: The second launch attempt was scrubbed when a liquid hydrogen leak was detected at the quick-disconnect fitting on the core stage engine section. Teams attempted three remediation methods — warming, chilling, and helium repressurization — all failed to seal the leak. Launch Director Charlie Blackwell-Thompson called the scrub at 11:17 AM EDT. The vehicle was subsequently rolled back to the VAB for repairs.

sources.name: CBS News Artemis I September Scrub

events.title: Artemis I Launches — First SLS/Orion Flight
events.detail: Artemis I lifted off from Launch Complex 39B at 01:47:44 UTC (8:47 PM EST November 15), generating approximately 8.8 million pounds of thrust — 15% more than Saturn V. Ten CubeSats were deployed after trans-lunar injection. This was the first flight of SLS, the first integrated flight of SLS and Orion together, and the first NASA deep-space human-rated spacecraft launch since Apollo 17 in December 1972.

events.title: Orion Performs First Powered Lunar Flyby — 80 Miles from Surface
events.detail: Orion performed its first powered flyby of the Moon, passing within 80 miles (130 km) of the lunar surface. The flyby burn inserted the capsule into a Distant Retrograde Orbit around the Moon. This was the closest any human-rated spacecraft had come to the Moon since the Apollo 17 command module in 1972.

events.title: Orion Sets Distance Record — 268,563 Miles from Earth
events.detail: Orion reached its farthest point from Earth: 268,563 miles (432,210 km), setting a distance record for any spacecraft designed to carry humans — surpassing the Apollo 13 record. The spacecraft had been in a Distant Retrograde Orbit around the Moon for six days at this point. All systems performed nominally in the deep-space radiation environment.

events.title: Artemis I Splashdown — Mission Complete (25.5 Days, 1.4M Miles)
events.detail: Orion splashed down in the Pacific Ocean west of Baja California at 9:40 AM PST — exactly 50 years to the day after Apollo 17's Moon landing. The mission covered 2.3 million kilometers (1.4 million miles) over 25.5 days. Post-recovery inspections later revealed unexpected charring on the Avcoat heat shield, triggering a major investigation that would delay Artemis II by over a year.

events.title: Blue Origin Wins Second HLS Contract — $3.4 Billion for Blue Moon Mk.2
events.detail: Under the Sustaining Lunar Development (SLD) program, NASA awarded Blue Origin a $3.4 billion firm-fixed-price contract to develop the Blue Moon Mk.2 crewed lander for Artemis V. This gave NASA two competing HLS providers. Blue Moon must complete an uncrewed landing demonstration before any crewed Artemis V mission. The contract ended the sole-source SpaceX arrangement and increased NASA's architecture redundancy.

events.title: Artemis II Crew Announced: Wiseman, Glover, Koch, Hansen
events.detail: NASA Administrator Bill Nelson announced the four-person Artemis II crew at Ellington Field, Houston: Commander Reid Wiseman (NASA), Pilot Victor Glover (NASA, first person of color to fly to deep space), Mission Specialist Christina Koch (NASA, first woman on a lunar trajectory), and Mission Specialist Jeremy Hansen (CSA, first non-American on a lunar trajectory and Hansen's first spaceflight). The crew would fly a 10-day crewed lunar flyby mission.

events.title: India Signs Artemis Accords During Modi State Visit
events.detail: During Prime Minister Modi's state visit to Washington, India became a signatory of the Artemis Accords — a significant diplomatic win given ISRO's growing capabilities. India's inclusion strengthened the accords as a counterweight to China's space ambitions and reflected the broader Indo-US strategic partnership. The accords had grown to over 26 signatories by this point.

events.title: NASA Launches 121-Test Heat Shield Investigation at Ames
events.detail: Following post-flight inspections of the Artemis I Orion capsule revealing unexpected charring and material loss on the Avcoat heat shield, NASA launched an eight-campaign, 121-test investigation at NASA Ames Arc Jet Complex. Root cause was eventually traced to lower-than-expected heating rates during skip reentry, which allowed gases to build up in the Avcoat layers, causing cracking and shedding. The investigation ran through December 2023 and directly drove Artemis II delays.

events.title: Starship Reaches Orbital Trajectory on IFT-3 — Key HLS Milestone
events.detail: SpaceX's Starship/Super Heavy reached its target orbital trajectory for the first time on Integrated Flight Test 3 (IFT-3). A critical Artemis milestone was achieved during this flight: Starship performed an internal cryogenic propellant transfer between tanks — a precursor to the ship-to-ship orbital refueling required for HLS operations. An estimated 14+ tanker flights would be needed to fuel Starship HLS for a lunar mission.

events.title: Artemis II Delayed to Late 2025; Artemis III Pushed to 2026
events.detail: NASA officially announced the first major schedule slip: Artemis II pushed from late 2024 to 'no earlier than September 2025,' primarily due to the heat shield char loss requiring trajectory redesign and Orion battery issues — four Eaglepicher 120V Li-ion batteries required disassembly and replacement to tolerate abort system environments. Twenty-four electrical power anomalies traced to radiation effects required software workarounds. Artemis III was pushed from 2025 to late 2026.

sources.name: NASA OIG Artemis II Readiness Report May 2024

events.title: NASA Cancels VIPER Lunar Rover Despite Near-Completion
events.detail: NASA cancelled the Volatiles Investigating Polar Exploration Rover (VIPER) despite the rover being nearly complete, citing cost overruns and schedule delays. VIPER was designed to prospect for water ice at the lunar south pole — directly supporting Artemis surface operations. The cancellation drew sharp criticism from the planetary science community, who viewed it as prioritizing the crewed Artemis architecture over science. The completed rover was subsequently offered for sale.

events.title: Artemis II Delayed Again to April 2026; Artemis III to Mid-2027
events.detail: NASA announced a second major delay. Artemis II was pushed from September 2025 to April 2026. Artemis III was pushed from late 2026 to mid-2027. The root cause of the heat shield anomaly was confirmed: skip reentry's lower-than-expected heating rates allowed gas pressure buildup in Avcoat, causing cracking. NASA's resolution was to modify the reentry trajectory rather than replace the heat shield material — a significant design change.

events.title: Artemis Accords Surpass 50 Signatory Nations
events.detail: The Artemis Accords surpassed 50 signatory nations, with representatives across Europe, Asia, South America, Africa, and Oceania. Notable additions included Rwanda and Nigeria (first African nations in 2022), France, Saudi Arabia, and India. By January 2026, Oman's accession brought the total to 61 nations. China and Russia remained outside the framework, advancing their own lunar exploration program independently.

events.title: Blue Origin's New Glenn Reaches Orbit on Maiden Flight
events.detail: Blue Origin's New Glenn heavy-lift rocket launched from Cape Canaveral Launch Complex 36 at 2:03 AM EST, carrying the Blue Ring Pathfinder payload to medium Earth orbit. New Glenn reached orbit on its first attempt — a rare achievement for a new rocket. The first stage booster was lost on the descent landing attempt at approximately Mach 5.5. The successful debut bolstered Blue Origin's credentials as a viable HLS provider for Artemis V.

events.title: Trump FY2026 Budget Proposes 24% NASA Cut — Largest in History
events.detail: The White House FY2026 budget request proposed cutting NASA from $24.8 billion to $18.8 billion — a $6 billion, 24.3% reduction and the largest single-year cut in NASA history. Key proposals: cancel SLS and Orion after Artemis III; cancel Gateway; cut science by 47%. A new 'Commercial Moon to Mars Infrastructure' program at $864 million was proposed as a commercial-first replacement. Both House and Senate appropriations committees ultimately rejected the most severe cuts.

events.title: Senate Confirms Jared Isaacman as 15th NASA Administrator
events.detail: The Senate confirmed Jared Isaacman — billionaire entrepreneur and Crew Dragon commander of Inspiration4 and Polaris Dawn — as the 15th NASA Administrator with a 67-30 vote. Sworn in on December 18, Isaacman became one of the few NASA administrators with personal spaceflight experience. He immediately initiated an architecture review of the Artemis program, flagging unsustainable costs and schedule overruns.

events.title: Artemis II Crew Practices Full Launch Countdown at KSC
events.detail: The four Artemis II astronauts — Reid Wiseman, Victor Glover, Christina Koch, and Jeremy Hansen — practiced the full launch countdown procedure at Kennedy Space Center as part of final crew readiness preparations for the April 2026 launch target. This included suit-up, ingress drills, and communications checks in the Orion capsule atop the SLS rocket.

sources.name: Spaceflight Now Artemis II Countdown Practice

events.title: Artemis II Delayed Again by Liquid Hydrogen Leak During WDR
events.detail: During a pre-launch wet dress rehearsal tanking test, a liquid hydrogen fuel leak was discovered at the base of SLS. Additional issues included a faulty valve on Orion, audio communication problems, and cold-weather camera failures. Launch was pushed from late February to March or later, adding to the growing list of Artemis II delays. SLS Program Manager John Honeycutt noted the 3+ year gap between launches increased the risk of encountering issues.

sources.name: Aerospace America Artemis II WDR Issues

events.title: SLS Rolled Back to VAB for Helium Supply Line Blockage
events.detail: NASA's crawler-transporter 2 returned the fully stacked Artemis II SLS/Orion to the Vehicle Assembly Building to troubleshoot a blockage in the helium supply line to the ICPS (Interim Cryogenic Propulsion Stage) upper stage. The rollback effectively ruled out any March launch windows. A new fueling test was planned upon the vehicle's return to the pad, with an April or later target for launch.

sources.name: Spaceflight Now Artemis II VAB Rollback

events.title: NASA Cancels Exploration Upper Stage; ULA Centaur V Selected
events.detail: NASA announced the cancellation of the Exploration Upper Stage and the SLS Block 1B and Block 2 upgrade programs. SLS will continue in a standardized Block 1 configuration. NASA confirmed a contract with United Launch Alliance to use the Centaur V as a replacement upper stage for future SLS flights, formally confirmed by contract on March 7, 2026. This ended Boeing's multi-year EUS development program and wrote off approximately $2.8 billion in development investment.

sources.name: Spaceflight Now ULA Centaur V Contract

events.title: Isaacman Announces Major Artemis Architecture Overhaul
events.detail: NASA Administrator Jared Isaacman announced a sweeping restructuring of the Artemis program: Artemis III (now targeting 2027) redefined as a low-Earth orbit rendezvous and docking test — NOT a Moon landing; Artemis IV (targeting 2028) designated as the first actual crewed lunar landing; at least one surface landing per year thereafter. The Lunar Gateway was cancelled from early Artemis architecture. Both SpaceX and Blue Origin concurred with the new approach. Congressional stakeholders were briefed and expressed support.

events.title: Isaacman Outlines Post-Overhaul Architecture Details
events.detail: In a one-on-one interview, NASA Administrator Isaacman discussed Artemis II launch progress, NASA OIG readiness report responses, workforce planning, and upcoming milestones. He reiterated his target of two lunar landings in 2028, confirmed continued development of both SpaceX Starship HLS and Blue Origin Blue Moon Mk.2 landers, and indicated further details on the revised post-Artemis III architecture would be forthcoming in coming weeks.

events.title: Artemis II Crew Enters Quarantine; Rollout to LC-39B Finalized
events.detail: NASA finalized the Artemis II rollout schedule and the four-person crew — Commander Reid Wiseman, Pilot Victor Glover, Mission Specialist Christina Koch, and Mission Specialist Jeremy Hansen — began their pre-launch quarantine at Johnson Space Center in Houston. Two days later, on March 20, crawler-transporter 2 carried the fully stacked SLS and Orion to Launch Complex 39B at 11:21 a.m. EDT, completing an 11-hour, 4-mile journey from the Vehicle Assembly Building. The launch is targeted no earlier than April 1, 2026 at 6:24 p.m. EDT, the first crewed mission to a lunar trajectory since Apollo 17 in 1972.

sources.name: NASA Blog: Artemis II Rollout Crew Begins Quarantine (Mar 18, 2026)
NASA Blog: Artemis II Rocket Arrives at LC-39B (Mar 20, 2026)
Space.com: Artemis 2 Moon Rocket Rollout Coverage (Mar 20, 2026)

events.title: NASA 'Ignition' Event: Lunar Gateway Cancelled, $20B Permanent Moon Base Announced
events.detail: NASA Administrator Jared Isaacman hosted the 'Ignition' event, formally cancelling the Lunar Gateway space station 'in its current form' and announcing a $20 billion, 7-year plan to build a permanent lunar surface base instead. The plan envisions 76 landings delivering over 200 metric tons of hardware — habitats, nuclear power systems, rovers, drones, and in-situ resource utilization equipment — with sustained human surface presence after 2032. International partners ESA, JAXA, and CSA were reportedly surprised; ESA said it is 'consulting closely with Member States.' Isaacman cited urgency vs. China: 'The difference between success and failure will be measured in months, not years.' NASA declared it is 'confident it has the funds' for the new program.

sources.name: CNBC: NASA Cancels Gateway, Announces $20B Moon Base (Mar 24, 2026)

Bloomberg: Isaacman on Moon Base Funding (Mar 24, 2026)

events.title: Artemis II Launches — First Humans Beyond Low Earth Orbit Since Apollo 17
events.detail: NASA's SLS Block 1 rocket carrying the Orion spacecraft (callsign: Integrity) lifted off from LC-39B at Kennedy Space Center at 6:35:12 p.m. EDT on April 1, 2026 — the first crewed mission beyond low Earth orbit since Apollo 17 in December 1972. The crew: Commander Reid Wiseman, Pilot Victor Glover (first person of color beyond LEO), Mission Specialist Christina Koch (first woman on a lunar trajectory), and Mission Specialist Jeremy Hansen (CSA, first non-American beyond LEO). The 10-day mission will send the crew on a free-return trajectory around the Moon without entering lunar orbit. Two brief holds during the countdown were resolved: a Flight Termination System ground hardware issue and a Launch Abort System battery sensor anomaly (instrumentation fault). All systems performed nominally; solar arrays fully deployed. Weather was 90% favorable at launch.

sources.name: NASA Artemis Blog: Live Artemis II Launch Day Updates (Apr 1, 2026)
CNN: Artemis II launch live updates — Moon mission lifts off (Apr 1, 2026)
NASASpaceFlight.com: Artemis II returns humanity to the Moon (Apr 1, 2026)

events.title: Artemis II Completes Historic Lunar Flyby — Sets New Human Deep Space Distance Record at 252,706 Miles
events.detail: Flight Day 6 of Artemis II delivered one of the most significant milestones in human spaceflight since the Apollo era. At 1:56 p.m. EDT, Orion surpassed Apollo 13's 1970 record of 248,655 miles from Earth — making Wiseman, Glover, Koch, and Hansen the farthest-traveling humans in history at 252,706 miles maximum distance. The lunar flyby observation window ran from 2:45 p.m. to 9:40 p.m. EDT; closest approach occurred at approximately 7:02 p.m. EDT at 4,070 miles above the lunar surface. The crew observed and photographed 30 pre-selected lunar targets including the Orientale basin (~600 miles wide, formed ~3.8 billion years ago), polar terrain, and candidate landing sites for future Artemis missions. The flyby provided unprecedented human visual observation of the lunar far side and south pole region. All Orion systems remained nominal; crew was in excellent health.

sources.name: NASA Artemis Blog: Flight Day 6 — Crew Ready for Lunar Flyby (Apr 6, 2026)
NPR: NASA's Artemis II crew flies around the Moon (Apr 6, 2026)
CNN: Why Artemis II's lunar flyby offers unprecedented views (Apr 6, 2026)

events.title: Artemis II Splashdown — Mission Complete After 10-Day Historic Lunar Flyby
events.detail: Orion splashed down off the coast of San Diego, California at approximately 8:07 p.m. EDT on April 10, 2026, completing humanity's first crewed lunar flyby in over 50 years. The Orion capsule executed a skip-reentry trajectory — the modified approach validated after the Artemis I heat shield anomaly — decelerating from lunar return speed before parachute deployment at approximately 6,000 feet, with the three main chutes fully deployed at 8:04 p.m. EDT. The USS John P. Murtha recovered the crew. Commander Reid Wiseman, Pilot Victor Glover, Mission Specialist Christina Koch, and Mission Specialist Jeremy Hansen were extracted from Orion within two hours of splashdown and flown to Johnson Space Center. The 10-day mission accomplished all primary objectives: validating Orion life support for crewed deep-space flight, testing the Orion Crew Survival System suits in microgravity, demonstrating manual piloting in deep space, and collecting scientific imagery of 30 lunar surface targets. The modified skip-reentry data directly enables Artemis IV's crewed lunar landing.

sources.name: NBC News: Artemis II splashdown — crew returns to Earth (Apr 10, 2026)

events.title: Artemis II Crew Returns to Houston — JSC Homecoming Ceremony
events.detail: The four-person Artemis II crew flew to Ellington Field at NASA's Johnson Space Center in Houston on April 11, greeted by hundreds of employees, military officers, and the full astronaut corps. Commander Reid Wiseman: 'We are bonded forever — no one down here is ever going to know what the four of us just went through.' Victor Glover: 'I have not processed what we just did and I'm afraid to start even trying.' Christina Koch: 'Earth was just this lifeboat hanging undisturbedly in the universe.' Canadian astronaut Jeremy Hansen spoke of the mission belonging to all humanity. The crew began post-flight medical reconditioning at JSC. Orion was secured aboard the USS John P. Murtha for transport to Naval Base San Diego, then Kennedy Space Center, for a 30-day post-flight inspection.

sources.name: NASA Blog: Artemis II Astronauts Back in Houston (Apr 11, 2026)
Space.com: Artemis 2 astronauts describe their epic moon mission (Apr 11, 2026)

events.title: Orion Post-Flight Analysis Begins — 30-Day Heat Shield Inspection Underway
events.detail: NASA began formal post-flight analysis of the Orion spacecraft as the USS John P. Murtha recovery vessel headed to Naval Base San Diego. Heat shield specialists began examining the Avcoat ablative material — initial visual inspection showed expected wear but no catastrophic damage, suggesting the modified skip-reentry trajectory successfully mitigated the Artemis I char loss anomaly. Orion will be returned to Kennedy Space Center for a 30-day inspection, with a comprehensive heat shield report expected to directly inform whether the Artemis IV crewed lunar landing timeline (targeting 2028) can be confirmed. Congressional leaders praised the mission's success. House Science Committee Chairman Brian Babin: 'For the first time in more than 50 years, American astronauts traveled beyond low Earth orbit, showcasing the ingenuity, determination, and pioneering spirit that define our nation.'

sources.name: TMJ4/AP: Heat shield data from Artemis II could define Artemis IV timeline (Apr 2026)
House Science Committee: Chairman Babin statement on Artemis II (Apr 2026)

events.title: Artemis II Crew Holds Official Postflight News Conference at JSC
events.detail: The four Artemis II astronauts held their official postflight news conference at NASA's Johnson Space Center at 2:30 p.m. EDT. Commander Wiseman, Pilot Glover, Mission Specialists Koch and Hansen discussed mission accomplishments including manual piloting in deep space, record-setting lunar photography, and the emotional experience of returning to lunar distance for the first time since Apollo 17. The conference provided the first comprehensive public debrief of mission data. NASA reiterated that results from the ongoing 30-day Orion heat shield inspection at KSC will directly inform the Artemis IV crewed landing timeline.

sources.name: NASA News Release: Artemis II Crew Postflight News Conference
WKNO FM: NASA's Artemis II News Conference with Moon Astronauts

events.title: Mobile Launcher 1 Rolls to VAB — Artemis III Stacking Campaign Begins
events.detail: NASA's Mobile Launcher 1 began rolling from Launch Complex 39B back to the Vehicle Assembly Building at 8:11 a.m. EDT on Crawler-Transporter 2 — a 4-mile trek signaling the formal end of Artemis II launch pad operations and start of Artemis III campaign activities. Teams will perform checkouts, inspections, and repairs on ML-1 before beginning SLS stacking for Artemis III. The Artemis III mission — now redesignated as a low-Earth orbit Starship HLS rendezvous and docking test rather than a lunar landing — is targeted for launch in 2027. The rollout is a key milestone in maintaining the Artemis launch cadence toward the Artemis IV crewed lunar landing target of 2028.

sources.name: NASA Artemis Blog: Mobile Launcher Rolls Ahead of Artemis III Preparation

events.title: Mobile Launcher 1 Arrives at VAB — Artemis III Infrastructure Secured
events.detail: NASA's Mobile Launcher 1 completed its approximately 4-mile journey from LC-39B, arriving at the Vehicle Assembly Building at 11:40 a.m. EDT after departing the previous morning. At the VAB, teams will perform checkouts, inspections, and repairs on the tower — which sustained minor damage during Artemis II's April 1 launch — before stacking Artemis III hardware. ML-1's arrival formally closes the Artemis II ground campaign and opens the Artemis III ground operations phase.

sources.name: NASA Blog: Mobile Launcher Arrives at Vehicle Assembly Building
Yahoo News: NASA rolls back mobile launcher for Artemis III

events.title: Artemis III SLS Core Stage Rolls Out at Michoud — Manufacturing Milestone
events.detail: NASA's Michoud Assembly Facility in New Orleans hosted the rollout of the 'top four-fifths' of the Artemis III SLS core stage — liquid hydrogen tank, intertank, liquid oxygen tank, engine section, and core stage avionics — as the rocket hardware prepares for transport to Stennis Space Center for engine testing and eventual integration at KSC. The milestone marks significant manufacturing progress toward the Artemis III 2027 launch target and sustains hardware cadence needed for Artemis IV's 2028 crewed lunar landing.

sources.name: NASA: Media Invited to Artemis III Moon Rocket Stage Rollout
Space Policy Online: NASA Rollout of Artemis III SLS Rocket

events.title: NASA Initial Assessments: Artemis II Orion Heat Shield Performed 'Significantly Better' Than Artemis I
events.detail: NASA published its initial post-mission assessment of Artemis II, confirming that Orion is on track for future missions. Key findings: the Avcoat heat shield performed 'significantly better' than Artemis I under the modified skip-reentry trajectory designed after the Artemis I char-loss anomaly; SLS placed Orion at over 18,000 mph at main engine cutoff; the launch pad sustained minimal damage. Orion returned to Kennedy Space Center's Multi-Payload Processing Facility for a formal 30-day heat shield inspection. Sample extractions and Marshall Space Flight Center X-ray scans will follow. Findings are expected ~May 10 and will determine whether the Artemis IV crewed lunar landing timeline (2028) can be confirmed as planned.

sources.name: NASA: On Track for Future Missions with Initial Artemis II Assessments
Phys.org: NASA on track for future missions with initial Artemis II assessments

events.title: SpaceX Starship V3 Full-Stack Static Fires Complete — Flight 12 Targets Late April from Pad 2
events.detail: SpaceX completed all full-stack static fire milestones for Starship Flight 12: Ship 39 fired on April 14 and Booster 19 ignited all 33 Raptor 3 engines on April 15 at Starbase Pad 2 — the first time Pad 2 has supported pre-launch testing. Flight 12 will be the first Starship orbital launch from Pad 2 and the debut of the Starship Version 3 configuration. V3 uses redesigned Raptor 3 engines with higher thrust and improved reliability, and a reinforced heat shield tile system targeting more durable reentry performance. The vehicle is directly related to Artemis III HLS: SpaceX must demonstrate the V3 configuration's reliability and reentry capability before adapting the design for the crewed lunar-landing-capable Starship HLS variant required for Artemis missions from 2027 onward.

sources.name: Space Explored: Starship Flight 12 inches closer to launch with booster and ship static fires (Apr 18, 2026)

events.title: NASA Names Artemis III Crew — First ESA Astronaut Assigned to an Artemis Mission
events.detail: NASA announced the Artemis III crew at Johnson Space Center: Commander Randy Bresnik, ESA Pilot Luca Parmitano (the first ESA astronaut assigned to an Artemis mission), and Mission Specialists Frank Rubio and Andre Douglas, with Bob Hines as backup. The mission — redesignated in February 2026 as an Earth-orbit rendezvous/docking demonstration with SpaceX and Blue Origin HLS landers — targets a 2027 launch ahead of the first crewed lunar landing on Artemis IV (2028).

sources.name: NASA — NASA Marches Toward Artemis III Mission in 2027, Names Crew Members

events.title: ESA Council Reframes Gateway Contributions, Sets December Rome Ministerial
events.detail: Following NASA's March 2026 Gateway pause, ESA's 347th Council concluded that development of the Lunar I-Hab habitation module will continue to critical design review, Lunar View logistics/refueling activities will slow while preserving key technologies, and Lunar Link communications is being studied for integration into ESA's Moonlight constellation. Member states set a December 2026 Interim Ministerial in Rome to define Europe's exploration roadmap — a decision Director General Josef Aschbacher likened to the pivotal 2023 Seville Space Summit.

sources.name: ESA — Key outcomes of the 347th ESA Council meeting

events.title: Artemis III Hardware Assembly Accelerates — Heat Shield Installed, SRB Stacking Begins
events.detail: Less than three months after Artemis II's crew returned, Artemis III hardware processing accelerated at Kennedy Space Center: the Orion heat shield (186 individually inspected Avcoat blocks, incorporating post-Artemis-I design refinements) was installed on July 6, 2026, and the first solid rocket booster aft segments were secured to the mobile launcher inside the Vehicle Assembly Building on July 11, 2026, beginning the stacking campaign. Crew members Randy Bresnik and Andre Douglas visited Exploration Ground Systems teams at the booster segment on July 10.

sources.name: NASA — NASA's Artemis III Flight Hardware Stacks Up at Kennedy

events.title: NASA Selects SpaceX Starlink Laser Terminals for Artemis III Orion Communications
events.detail: NASA announced it selected SpaceX to install two Starlink mini laser communications terminals on Orion's exterior for Artemis III, enabling 4K video and imagery downlink to Mission Control at rates far exceeding Orion's existing radio-frequency systems as the crew tests rendezvous and docking with Starship and Blue Moon HLS test articles.

sources.name: NASA — NASA Taps SpaceX's Starlink to Deliver Artemis III Imagery from Orion

events.title: Final RS-25 Engine Delivered to KSC — All Four Artemis III Core Stage Engines Now on Site
events.detail: The fourth and final RS-25 engine for the Artemis III SLS core stage was delivered to the Vehicle Assembly Building at Kennedy Space Center on July 21, 2026, from NASA's Stennis Space Center. Technicians began integrating the engines with the core stage over the summer, running roughly four months ahead of the equivalent point in the Artemis II campaign.

sources.name: NASA — NASA Joins Artemis III Orion Modules; Rocket Hardware Update

events.title: Artemis III Orion Crew and Service Modules Joined at Kennedy Space Center
events.detail: Technicians joined the Orion crew module and service module for Artemis III on July 30, 2026, inside the Neil Armstrong Operations and Checkout Building. The crew module will carry astronauts Randy Bresnik, Andre Douglas, Frank Rubio, and ESA's Luca Parmitano; the European-built service module reuses more than 250 components from the Artemis II capsule. NASA said the combined spacecraft will next be powered on for the first time.

events.title: Four Commercial Moon Base Landers Clear Testing Milestones Simultaneously
events.detail: NASA announced that Blue Origin, Firefly Aerospace, Intuitive Machines, and Voyager Technologies each cleared major testing milestones for their Moon Base cargo landers around the same time: thermal-vacuum and comms checkouts (Blue Moon MK1 'Endurance'), autonomous landing sequence demo (Blue Ghost Mission 2/Elytra), long-range thermal-vacuum testing (IM-3 Nova-C), and mass-properties testing (Griffin-1). Voyager's Griffin-1 targets a late-2026 delivery; the other three target 2028.

sources.name: NASA — NASA Provides Updates on Moon Base Cargo Landers, Tech Demonstrations

events.title: Blue Origin Identifies BE-4 Valve Issue Behind New Glenn Explosion; Blue Moon Mark 1 Slips to Q1 2027
events.detail: Blue Origin CEO Dave Limp said the May 28, 2026 New Glenn static-fire explosion at LC-36 was caused by an issue with the main oxygen valve on a BE-4 engine. Modified hardware is expected by end of August 2026, but the debut of the Blue Moon Mark 1 lunar cargo lander — needed to deliver NASA's Moon Base I rovers — has slipped from late summer 2026 to Q1 2027 at the earliest, pending New Glenn's return to flight.

sources.name: Spaceflight Now — Blue Origin identifies engine issue behind New Glenn explosion

events.title: NASA Completes LEMS Seismometer Payload for Artemis Astronaut Deployment at Lunar South Pole
events.detail: NASA declared "wrenches down" on the Lunar Environment Monitoring Station (LEMS), the first fully completed science payload designed for Artemis astronauts to deploy on the Moon's surface. Built at NASA Goddard, the 11-pound instrument suite carries two seismometers for autonomous long-term monitoring of moonquakes and meteorite impacts near the lunar South Pole, and will await assignment to a specific Artemis surface mission in a Goddard clean room.

sources.name: NASA Science — NASA Completes Astronaut-Deployed Science Instrument for Lunar Surface

events.title: Study: AstroRad Vest Tested on Artemis I Could Cut Deep-Space Radiation Exposure Up to 60%
events.detail: A Science Advances study led by StemRad's Jordan Houri found the AstroRad radiation-shielding vest, flown unoccupied on Artemis I mannequins Helga and Zohar in 2022, could cut an astronaut's radiation dose by ~60% in a 1972-scale solar storm and ~40% in a 1989-scale event. The 26 kg vest was not carried on the crewed Artemis II flyby due to mass and space constraints but is being considered for longer lunar and Mars-bound crews.

sources.name: Phys.org (AP) — Radiation vest tested on NASA moonshot can cut astronauts' exposure in solar storms, study suggests

events.title: Artemis III SLS Booster Nose Cones Arrive at Vehicle Assembly Building
events.detail: The aerodynamic forward assemblies (nose cones) for the twin Artemis III SLS solid rocket boosters arrived at KSC's Vehicle Assembly Building, to be integrated atop the boosters inside High Bay 3 — continuing SRB stacking that began in early July, roughly four months ahead of the equivalent point in Artemis II's campaign.

sources.name: Friends of NASA — NASA Artemis III SLS Solid Rocket Boosters

events.title: Isaacman: "Extremely Confident" Artemis III Launches in 2027, Details Three-Launch Sequence
events.detail: NASA Administrator Jared Isaacman said he is "extremely confident" Artemis III launches in 2027, detailing the mission's three-launch order: Blue Origin's New Glenn flies first with a Blue Moon Mark 2 test lander (life support and crew habitation installed), followed days later by SLS/Orion, then SpaceX's Starship V3 with a docking adapter. He called SpaceX's rising launch cadence — an early-September flight and roughly biweekly launches through year-end — critical to the schedule.

sources.name: Spaceflight Now — NASA Administrator 'extremely confident' in Artemis 3 mission in 2027

events.title: Gateway's HALO Module Repurposed Into Three Lunar Infrastructure Demo Missions; Canada Redirects Canadarm3
events.detail: Following the March 2026 cancellation of the Lunar Gateway as a stepping-stone architecture, NASA and Northrop Grumman announced the cancelled HALO (Habitation and Logistics Outpost) module — which had absorbed roughly $1.9B in contract value since its 2019 award — will be converted into three Lunar Infrastructure Demo (LID-1/2/3) missions reusing HALO-derived power, thermal, autonomy and communications hardware to mature systems that can survive the lunar night near the South Pole, feeding directly into Moon Base Phase I (through 2029). The same day, the Canadian Space Agency announced it would repurpose its Canadarm3 robotic-arm investment — built on 25 years of Canadarm2 ISS heritage — for Artemis lunar surface operations and potential commercial LEO stations rather than the cancelled Gateway.
